findings.title: Async legacy writes inherit the request context and are cancelled on return
findings.body: Create, Delete, Update, and DeleteCollection start the legacy write in a goroutine with context.WithTimeoutCause(ctx, 10s). That child is still cancelled as soon as the incoming request context is cancelled, which happens when the handler returns the unified-storage result. The 10s timeout never applies. The legacy "safe measure" write is therefore raced against request completion and will usually fail with context.Canceled, so legacy storage diverges from unified storage with no retry. Derive the background work from context.WithoutCancel (then apply the timeout), and log the legacy error instead of only recording a metric.

findings.title: Legacy Update reuses the same UpdatedObjectInfo concurrently
findings.body: After Storage.Update returns, the goroutine calls Legacy.Update with the same objInfo value. UpdatedObjectInfo implementations typically cache the computed object or mutate internal state on the first UpdatedObject call, and Storage.Update may still be using that state. Running both updates at once races on that shared object and no longer writes the unified-storage result into legacy (the previous code snapshotted the updated object and applied that exact object to legacy). Legacy can fail optimistic concurrency, apply a different patch, or panic, so the two stores diverge.

findings.title: Successful Delete records the object name as the metric kind label
findings.body: On the Delete success path, recordStorageDuration is called with name (the object name) where every other call passes options.Kind. If that argument is a Prometheus label, each deleted object creates a new series and cardinality grows without bound. The error path on the previous line correctly uses options.Kind, so success and failure are also not comparable.

findings.title: Storage failures and legacy delete-collection are recorded on the wrong histogram
findings.body: Create and Update record a storage error with recordLegacyDuration (lines 45 and 129), so a unified-storage failure is counted as a legacy-storage failure and is missing from the storage histogram. DeleteCollection's async legacy call (line 166) uses recordStorageDuration instead of recordLegacyDuration, so legacy delete-collection latency and errors are attributed to unified storage. Mode 3 latency/error dashboards will be wrong and can hide a broken legacy backfill.

findings.title: Destroy does not wait for in-flight legacy goroutines
findings.body: Destroy closes Storage and Legacy immediately while Create/Update/Delete/DeleteCollection may still be running legacy writes in detached goroutines. Those calls can hit a destroyed backend (panic or lost write) during shutdown or mode switch, and there is no way for the caller to know the backfill finished.

findings.title: Mode 3 tests never observe the async legacy write and mock the wrong store on errors
findings.body: The Create error case is named as a unified-storage failure but only stubs Legacy.Create, and Storage.Create has no expectation, so the test does not exercise the path it claims. Success cases start legacy work in a goroutine and return without AssertCalled, a wait, or AssertExpectations, so a missing or panicked legacy write still passes. The playlist mode 3 integration test then reads the legacy API immediately after a k8s write, which will flake or fail for the same unsynchronized async path.
